title: Basic Electricity and Circuits
summary: Learn current, voltage, resistance, Ohm's law, series and parallel circuits, power and cost, and safe practice, with worked calculations.
audience: Students, apprentices, technicians and curious learners

body.p: Electricity is the flow of electric charge. In metal wires the charge carriers are electrons. Current is the rate of flow of charge and is measured in amperes (A). Voltage, also called potential difference, is the push that drives the current and is measured in volts (V). Resistance is the opposition to current and is measured in ohms (Ω).

Think of a water pipe. Voltage is like water pressure, current is like the amount of water flowing per second, and resistance is like a narrow pipe that restricts the flow. A battery or power supply acts like the pump.

list: Conductors such as copper and aluminium let current flow easily.
Insulators such as rubber, glass and plastic block current.
Direct current (DC) flows one way, as from a battery.
Alternating current (AC) changes direction many times a second, as from the mains. Mains frequency is 50 Hz in most of Africa and Europe.

body.tip: Always treat mains electricity as dangerous. Voltages above about 50 V can cause serious injury.

body.p: Ohm's law links voltage, current and resistance: V = I × R. Voltage in volts equals current in amperes times resistance in ohms. Rearranged, I = V ÷ R and R = V ÷ I.

list: A 12 V battery drives current through a 4 Ω resistor. I = 12 ÷ 4 = 3 A.
A heater on 230 V draws 5 A. Its resistance is 230 ÷ 5 = 46 Ω.
A current of 2 A flows through 3 Ω. The voltage across it is 2 × 3 = 6 V.

body.p: Ohm's law holds for most metal conductors at constant temperature. Components such as diodes and light bulbs do not follow it exactly, because their resistance changes.

body.tip: Write the formula, substitute the numbers with their units, then calculate. Check that your answer is reasonable.

body.p: In a series circuit, components are connected end to end so the same current flows through all of them. The total resistance is the sum: R = R1 + R2 + R3. Two resistors of 10 Ω and 20 Ω in series give 10 + 20 = 30 Ω. If one component breaks, the whole circuit stops.

In a parallel circuit, components are on separate branches across the same voltage. Current splits between branches. The total resistance is found from 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2. Two 10 Ω resistors in parallel give 1/R = 1/10 + 1/10 = 2/10, so R = 5 Ω. Total resistance in parallel is always less than the smallest branch.

list: Series: same current, voltages add up.
Parallel: same voltage, currents add up.
Household sockets and lights are wired in parallel so each works independently.

body.tip: Use a fuse or circuit breaker in series with the supply. It cuts the current if a fault causes too much flow.

body.p: Electrical power is the rate of using energy. It is measured in watts (W) and calculated as P = V × I. A device on 230 V that draws 5 A uses 230 × 5 = 1,150 W. Using Ohm's law, power can also be written as P = I² × R or P = V² ÷ R.

Energy used is power multiplied by time. The common unit on electricity bills is the kilowatt-hour (kWh): one kilowatt of power used for one hour. A 1,500 W heater used for 3 hours uses 1.5 × 3 = 4.5 kWh. If a unit costs 150 per kWh, the cost is 4.5 × 150 = 675.

list: Switch off devices you are not using.
Choose LED bulbs, which give the same light for far less power.
Check the power rating label on appliances before connecting them.

body.p: Electricity can cause shocks, burns and fires. A shock happens when current flows through the body. Even small currents can be dangerous, and the risk is higher if skin is wet. Always switch off and isolate the supply before working on any circuit, and never work on mains wiring unless you are trained and licensed.

list: Fuse or circuit breaker: stops the current when it is too high.
Earthing: gives fault current a safe path to the ground, so metal casings do not stay live.
Residual current device (RCD): cuts the supply fast if current leaks to earth.
Insulation and correct cable size: thin cables overheat when they carry too much current.

body.p: Colour codes for cables differ between countries and have changed over time, so always check the code used where you live. Never assume a wire is dead. Test it with a suitable meter first.

body.tip: If someone is being shocked, switch off the supply first, or push them away with a dry non-conducting object. Then call for help.

body.p: A multimeter measures voltage, current and resistance. To measure voltage, place the meter in parallel across a component. To measure current, place the meter in series so the current flows through it. To measure resistance, switch off the power first and measure the component on its own.

list: Check the obvious first: is it plugged in, switched on, and is the fuse intact?
Measure the supply voltage at the device.
Check continuity with the meter on the resistance or buzzer setting. A broken wire shows very high resistance.
Replace faulty parts with the same rating.

body.p: Keep a record of what you measured and changed. This helps you find a repeating fault and shows exactly what you did if someone else takes over the job.

body.tip: Start with the largest range on a meter when you do not know the size of the quantity, then reduce it for a more accurate reading.
